title: The Afghan Peace Process
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: The history of Afghanistan includes many peace processes. After the US invasion, a meeting in Bonn led to a new government. This meeting was called a victor peace because the Taliban were not invited to take part.
pages.caption: US representative Zalmay Khalilzad (left) and Taliban representative Abdul Ghani Baradar (right) sign the US–Taliban deal in Doha, Qatar on 29 February 2020.

imageProvenance.credit: U.S. Department of State from United States

evidence.fileTitle: File:Secretary Pompeo Participates in a Signing Ceremony in Doha (49601220548).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: US representative Zalmay Khalilzad (left) and Taliban representative Abdul Ghani Baradar (right) sign the US–Taliban deal in Doha, Qatar on 29 February 2020.

pages.text: Leaving the Taliban out caused big problems. It led to a long insurgency. The peace agreement also gave a lot of power to warlords. Many people suffered because human rights were not a high priority.

Programs tried to disarm fighters and help them return to normal life. Japan helped coordinate this work. However, the programs faced trouble with ghost soldiers and illegal armed groups that stayed active.

Local peace deals happened in places like Helmand province. Some local agreements included written rules. Even so, many local deals failed because the national government and international forces did not support them.
Groups of citizens started nonviolent peace movements. In 2018, the People's Peace Movement marched across the country. They walked through dangerous areas to ask for a ceasefire and end the war.
Later, talks in Doha led to a deal with the United States. US forces withdrew from the country. Soon after, the Afghan Army collapsed, and the Taliban took control of Kabul in August 2021.

Efforts to bring peace to Afghanistan span several decades, featuring various national agreements and local initiatives. Following the 2001 United States invasion, the Bonn Conference produced an agreement widely described as a victor's peace.

imageProvenance.credit: U.S. Department of State from United States

pages.text: Because the Taliban were excluded and US military aims constrained the conference, human rights and transitional justice were given low priority. This exclusion empowered regional warlords and contributed directly to the subsequent Taliban insurgency.

Programs focused on disarmament, demobilization, and reintegration were implemented to disarm former fighters. While they successfully collected heavy weapons, they struggled with fictitious ghost soldiers and failed to break command structures.

Local peace processes occurred in Helmand province, such as in Musa Qala and Sangin. These local agreements faced difficulties and often collapsed due to opposition from the national government and foreign military actions.

Grassroots nonviolent resistance movements emerged to pressure both the government and the Taliban for ceasefires. Notably, the People's Peace Movement organized a long peace march across Afghanistan in 2018 to demand peace.
Negotiations later took place in Doha between the United States and the Taliban. These talks led to the withdrawal of US forces, the collapse of the Afghan Army, and the Fall of Kabul in August 2021.

Following the 2021 takeover, violent resistance continued across the country. Institutions like the United States Institute of Peace argued that a sustainable peace process remained necessary amid ongoing conflicts.

Efforts toward conflict resolution in Afghanistan have historically involved complex interactions between international interventions, national governance strategies, and grassroots civic movements. The 2001 Bonn Agreement established a political transition characterized as a victor's peace.

imageProvenance.credit: U.S. Department of State from United States

pages.text: The deliberate exclusion of the Taliban, compounded by the prioritization of foreign military objectives, marginalized transitional justice mechanisms. Consequently, this dynamic empowered factional commanders with documented records of human rights abuses and catalyzed the subsequent insurgency.

Structural efforts involving disarmament, demobilization, and reintegration encountered systemic obstacles. Although heavy weaponry was successfully confiscated, the initiatives failed to dismantle the underlying command networks of mid-level commanders, while administrative corruption inflated personnel metrics.

Parallel localized accommodations emerged in provinces like Helmand, attempting to negotiate localized ceasefires. These bottom-up arrangements frequently dissolved due to deficient institutional support from the national government and destabilizing military interventions.

Amid protracted warfare, civilian-led nonviolent movements mobilized to demand structural reforms and ceasefires. The People's Peace Movement, for instance, executed a prominent cross-country march in 2018 to advocate directly to belligerent factions.

Subsequent bilateral negotiations in Doha between the United States and the Taliban precipitated the withdrawal of international forces. This military exit preceded the rapid collapse of national defense forces and the seizure of Kabul in August 2021.

In the wake of the regime change, localized armed resistance persisted. Observers, including the United States Institute of Peace, maintained that comprehensive peace processes remained an essential requirement for regional stability.

title: Climate Politics and Policy History
sourceTitle: History of climate change policy and politics
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Climate change became a political topic in the 1970s. People wanted to find ways to solve global environmental problems. International policy started to focus on working together and making global guidelines. The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change is a major agreement that helps countries meet these new challenges.
pages.caption: National political divides on the seriousness of climate change consistently correlate with political ideology, with right-wing opinion being more negative.

evidence.fileTitle: File:20220831 Climate change is a "major threat" to my country - Pew survey.svg
evidence.articleCaption: National political divides on the seriousness of climate change consistently correlate with political ideology, with right-wing opinion being more negative.

pages.text: In the nineteenth century, people thought nature could not be changed by human actions. Books by writers like George Perkins Marsh and Aldo Leopold started to change how thinkers viewed human impact on nature. Later, in 1962, Rachel Carson wrote a book about pesticides that helped grow the global environmental movement.

Large-scale environmental actions began with Earth Day in 1970. Groups like Friends of the Earth were also founded that year. Activists called for better political actions to protect the planet. Later, major environmental groups started taking part in international discussions about climate policy.
pages.caption: Anthropogenic global warming—not global cooling or "imminent ice ages"—dominated peer-reviewed literature in the 1970s, contrary to false claims that climate science subsequently reversed its consensus.

evidence.fileTitle: File:1965-1979 Survey of scientific papers re global warming vs cooling.svg
evidence.articleCaption: Anthropogenic global warming—not global cooling or "imminent ice ages"—dominated peer-reviewed literature in the 1970s, contrary to false claims that climate science subsequently reversed its consensus.

pages.text: Efforts to deal with climate change often happened at a multinational level through the United Nations. The Montreal Protocol in 1987 showed that working together globally can work. Later, the Kyoto Protocol in 1997 set emission reduction rules for specific countries. The Paris Agreement followed in 2015 to continue these emission goals.

When international talks started, some thought talking about adaptation was a distraction from cutting emissions. Later, adaptation received more attention when reaching emission agreements proved difficult. Rich nations promised money to help developing nations with climate adaptation projects, and funding increased over the years.

Over time, political views on climate change became very divided. In the United States, political parties grew apart on the issue. While many people support action, large-scale citizen activism remained limited in the country, showing a gap between institutional progress and public engagement.

Climate change emerged as a political issue during the 1970s, as activists and formal organizations sought to address global environmental crises. International policy focused on cooperation and establishing guidelines such as the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, which developed continuously to tackle new challenges.

pages.text: Historically, Western thought viewed nature as unchanging and untouched by human influence. Nineteenth-century thinkers like George Perkins Marsh began challenging this narrative. Subsequent works by authors like Aldo Leopold and Rachel Carson drew attention to human impacts on ecosystems and wildlife, helping to create the modern environmental movement.

Global political discussions began in June 1972 at the UN Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm. Activism expanded significantly through events like Earth Day in 1970 and the creation of organizations such as Friends of the Earth. By the late 1980s, major environmental groups increasingly engaged in international climate campaigns.
pages.caption: Anthropogenic global warming—not global cooling or "imminent ice ages"—dominated peer-reviewed literature in the 1970s, contrary to false claims that climate science subsequently reversed its consensus.

pages.text: Multinational efforts under the United Nations aimed to reach consensus decisions. The 1987 Montreal Protocol demonstrated that this approach could work, though some critics favored bottom-up governance. The 1997 Kyoto Protocol set legally binding emission reduction commitments and defined flexibility mechanisms, while the 2015 Paris Agreement later succeeded it.

Initially, adaptation was viewed as an unwelcome distraction from mitigation efforts. However, limited progress at the Copenhagen Summit brought adaptation into focus during international negotiations. Rich nations committed to providing funds to help developing nations with adaptation projects, and funding increased between 2010 and 2020.

In the late 2000s, political discourse surrounding climate policy became increasingly polarizing. In the United States, a significant partisan gap emerged, with Democrats largely favoring priority action and Republicans largely opposing it. Despite institutional expansion and numerous organizations, large-scale citizen activism in the United States remained limited.

The trajectory of climate change policy encompasses ongoing political actions, regulatory trends, controversies, and activist initiatives. Emerging as a prominent political issue in the 1970s, international efforts centered on multilateral cooperation. Central to this architecture is the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, designed to evolve alongside emerging environmental challenges.

Nineteenth-century figures such as George Perkins Marsh initiated a narrative shift regarding human environmental impact. Subsequent ecological literature by authors like Aldo Leopold and Rachel Carson further catalyzed public awareness, laying foundational concepts for the broader environmental movement.

Formal political dialogue commenced with the 1972 Stockholm conference, establishing the necessity of cooperative state action. Concurrently, grassroots activism burgeoned with the inaugural Earth Day in 1970 and the establishment of advocacy groups like Friends of the Earth. By the late 1980s, these organizations transitioned from domestic advocacy to international campaigning within the UNFCCC framework.

pages.text: Multinational mitigation strategies historically relied on consensus-based UN frameworks, modeled after the successful Montreal Protocol, despite counter-proposals advocating bottom-up governance. The 1997 Kyoto Protocol established binding emission commitments and flexibility mechanisms for Annex 1 countries, eventually being succeeded by the 2015 Paris Agreement, which incorporated a long-term 1.5 °C target.

Adaptation policies initially encountered skepticism, dismissed as a distraction from primary mitigation objectives. However, subsequent diplomatic friction and limited progress at summits elevated adaptation on the agenda. Wealthy nations pledged financial assistance to support developing countries' adaptation projects, yielding an incremental increase in funding throughout the 2010–2020 decade despite unfulfilled overarching promises.

Political polarization regarding climate policy intensified during the late 2000s. In the United States, this manifested as a widening partisan divide in public opinion and legislative priorities. Furthermore, despite significant institutional expansion and numerous national organizations, sustained large-scale citizen mobilization remained constrained, highlighting a persistent divergence between institutional frameworks and public engagement.

title: Controlling the Coal Trade in England
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

A1-A2.headline: The Coal Cartel of Old England

pages.text: Long ago, a group of coal mine owners in north east England made a big price-fixing group. It was called the Limitation of the Vend. Their main buyers were ships that took the coal to other places.
pages.caption: Durham Cathedral (George Fennell Robson, British Museum). The Church was the biggest owner of coal-bearing lands.

imageProvenance.credit: George Fennel Robson (1788-1833), del.; William James Bennett (1782-1844) engraver

evidence.fileTitle: File:Durham Cathedral by Robson.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Durham Cathedral (George Fennell Robson, British Museum). The Church was the biggest owner of coal-bearing lands.

pages.text: London bought a huge amount of coal from the north east. The city was a voracious consumer of coal, needing it for domestic heating and manufacturing. As trees were cut down and firewood became scarce, Londoners gradually learned to burn coal indoors to keep warm.
The coal group worked out in the open. They had helpers to check if anyone broke the rules. They were never taken to court by the law, but Parliament looked into them many times.
Even though their prices were high, almost all the coal shipped to London came from this group. Their mines were near rivers that led straight out to the sea.
Transporting heavy coal by road was very costly. Water transport was much cheaper, so ships carried the heavy loads along the coast to the Thames river in London.
This special group stayed together for a very long time. Scholars still study how it worked because it was one of the most durable business cartels ever known.

B1-B2.headline: Controlling the Coal Trade in England

pages.text: The Limitation of the Vend operated as a historic price-fixing cartel formed by coal mine owners in north east England. While often dated from 1771 to 1845, its roots extended much further back in time.
pages.caption: Durham Cathedral (George Fennell Robson, British Museum). The Church was the biggest owner of coal-bearing lands.

imageProvenance.credit: George Fennel Robson (1788-1833), del.; William James Bennett (1782-1844) engraver

evidence.fileTitle: File:Durham Cathedral by Robson.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Durham Cathedral (George Fennell Robson, British Museum). The Church was the biggest owner of coal-bearing lands.

pages.text: Its primary customers were ship captains who purchased coal cargoes to resell across England, particularly in London. As the planet's first large mineral-fuelled city, London consumed vast amounts of coal to replace scarce firewood.

The cartel functioned openly through an organized secretariat that could usually detect cheating. Although participants believed their combination was legally questionable, they felt morally justified and were never successfully prosecuted by the law.

North east mines captured nearly the entire lucrative London market despite charging relatively high prices. Other nearby coalfields could rarely compete because the northern mines enjoyed exceptional sea-transport links via tidal rivers.

Moving heavy materials by road was prohibitively expensive as transport costs doubled within a few short miles. Conversely, navigable rivers flowing into the North Sea provided a much cheaper coastal route to the river Thames.

Unlike most business combinations that quickly collapsed due to internal cheating, the Limitation maintained itself for an exceptionally long period. Scholars continue to study its detailed records as one of the most fascinating economic history problems.

C1-C2.headline: The Limitation of the Vend Cartel

pages.text: The Limitation of the Vend constituted an enduring price-fixing cartel established by coal mine owners in County Durham and Northumberland. Although its active era is frequently dated 1771–1845, the arrangement possessed significantly earlier historical antecedents.
pages.caption: Durham Cathedral (George Fennell Robson, British Museum). The Church was the biggest owner of coal-bearing lands.

imageProvenance.credit: George Fennel Robson (1788-1833), del.; William James Bennett (1782-1844) engraver

evidence.fileTitle: File:Durham Cathedral by Robson.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Durham Cathedral (George Fennell Robson, British Museum). The Church was the biggest owner of coal-bearing lands.

pages.text: The cartel's principal market was London, a voracious consumer that had bypassed natural urban growth constraints by transitioning into a mineral-fuelled metropolis dependent on coal for domestic heating and diverse manufacturing processes.

Administered openly by a sophisticated secretariat capable of detecting internal defection, the cartel operated without legal prosecution, notwithstanding multiple parliamentary investigations and participants' apparent awareness of its questionable legality.

Despite maintaining elevated price structures, the cartel dominated the London market. Proximity to navigable tidal rivers furnished an insurmountable logistical advantage over rival coalfields, shielding the northern producers from effective undercutting.

The prohibitive expense of overland transport, which caused coal prices to double within a mere five to ten miles from the pit-head, rendered distant carriage economically unviable. This geographic reality elevated the utmost significance of the coastal shipping trade, wherein small sailing vessels transported bulky cargoes from the north east rivers across the North Sea toward the river Thames.

Surviving unusually long compared to typical business combinations plagued by defection, the cartel left meticulous records that continue to provide cliometric data for economic historians analyzing enduring monopoly behaviors.

title: Understanding Abrupt Climate Change
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Climate change can happen very fast. This means the climate system changes faster than normal. These fast changes are different from slow changes. They can happen because of things inside the climate system. Past events include the end of the Carboniferous rainforest collapse and the Younger Dryas.
pages.caption: Clathrate hydrates have been identified as a possible agent for abrupt changes.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Gashydrat mit Struktur.jpg

pages.text: Scientists study these events using different time ideas. Some events took a long time to start, while others happened quickly. For example, ice-cores show Greenland had a sudden warming of ten degrees Celsius within a few years long ago.

There are different ways to define these fast changes. Physics looks at how the climate shifts faster than outside forces. Impacts look at how fast changes cause trouble for human and natural systems. This second idea explains why people study these events so much.

Other fast events happened when glacial lakes drained quickly. The eight-point-two-kiloyear event happened because Glacial Lake Agassiz drained. Also, melting ice may have caused the Antarctic Cold Reversal about fourteen thousand five hundred years before present.

Feedback loops are a big part of fast climate change. A warming event can cause another change that adds to even more warming. Thawing permafrost is one example because it releases methane gas into the air. This makes the planet warm up faster.

Scientists use models to look at the future. Climate models predict that surface temperatures could leave the usual range of variability by the year 2047 if greenhouse gas emissions continue. Crossing critical thresholds could lead to large and fast changes.

Abrupt climate change happens when the climate system transitions at a rate determined by its own energy-balance. This change is more rapid than the external forcing driving it. Past events include the Younger Dryas and Dansgaard-Oeschger events. Today, the term also describes sudden shifts detectable within a human lifetime.

pages.text: Scientists define these events in terms of physics or impacts. Physically, the climate transitions faster than the responsible forcing. In terms of impacts, the change occurs so rapidly that human and natural systems struggle to adapt, which explains why researchers study these events extensively.

The timescales of these events vary significantly. Ice-cores from Greenland show a sudden warming of ten degrees Celsius within a few years at the end of the Younger Dryas. Other shifts include a six degree Celsius warming on Antarctica twenty-two thousand years ago.

Some abrupt changes are linked to the catastrophic draining of glacial lakes. The 8.2-kiloyear event is associated with the draining of Glacial Lake Agassiz. Additionally, rapid meltwater pulses from ice sheets likely caused the Antarctic Cold Reversal about fourteen thousand five hundred years ago.

Feedback processes can drive abrupt changes when a warming event triggers further warming. Thawing permafrost releases methane, a powerful greenhouse gas that holds twice as much carbon as the current atmosphere. Melting ice sheets also reduce Earth albedo, warming the planet faster.

Climate models project that under ongoing greenhouse gas emissions, near-surface temperatures could depart from the variability range of the last 150 years as early as 2047. When critical thresholds or tipping points are crossed, they lead to accelerating and often irreversible changes.

Abrupt climate change describes transitions in the climate system occurring at a rate dictated by internal energy-balances rather than external forcings. Historical instances range from the Younger Dryas to Heinrich events. Modern usage also encompasses rapid shifts detectable within human lifespans, often driven by internal feedbacks and system tipping points.

pages.text: Definitions partition into physical mechanics and societal impacts. Physically, the system reorganizes faster than the forcing mechanism. From an impact perspective, changes transpire too rapidly for natural and human systems to adapt, justifying the extensive research dedicated to these phenomena.

Observed timescales exhibit high variability. Greenland ice-core records demonstrate a ten degree Celsius warming within years at the termination of the Younger Dryas. Conversely, the onset duration of the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum spans from decades to millennia.

Catastrophic drainage of glacial lakes frequently instigates abrupt shifts. The 8.2-kiloyear event correlates with Glacial Lake Agassiz emptying, while meltwater pulses likely triggered the Antarctic Cold Reversal approximately 14,500 years before present. Circulation shifts, such as Meridional Overturning Circulation shutdowns, further illustrate past instability.

Feedback loops amplify these dynamics. Warming induces secondary alterations that exacerbate temperature anomalies, exemplified by permafrost thaw releasing significant methane reserves and glacier reduction diminishing planetary albedo. Higher warming magnitudes and prolonged durations elevate the probability of such abrupt transitions.

Earth system models project that continued greenhouse gas emissions could drive near-surface temperatures beyond the historical variability range of the past 150 years by 2047. Crossing critical tipping thresholds accelerates irreversible changes across ice sheets, ocean currents, and ecosystems.
